analysis.one_liner: Taxes trades of stocks, bonds, and derivatives, starting at 0.02% and rising to 0.1%.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in June 2025 with 10 Democratic cosponsors and referred to the House Ways and Means Committee, where it has not moved since.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would add a small tax on every purchase of a stock, bond, or derivative contract on US exchanges or by US persons. The rate starts at 0.02% of the trade's value in 2026 and gradually rises to 0.1% by 2030, meaning a $10,000 stock trade would eventually owe $10. High-frequency trading firms doing enormous volumes of small trades would pay the most, and the money raised would go to the Treasury like other federal revenue. Exchanges and brokers would collect the tax rather than individual investors.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers in general, since the tax would raise federal revenue from high-volume financial trading rather than from wages, and any trading costs passed to small investors are capped at a fraction of a percent per trade. The bill's backers, all progressive Democrats, frame it as making Wall Street contribute to public revenue. The tax would fall most heavily on high-frequency trading firms, hedge funds, and other institutional traders who turn over huge volumes.

how_it_helps.text: The bill imposes a tax on each covered purchase of a security, starting at 0.02% of the trade's value and rising in annual steps to 0.1% after 2029 [S2].
The tax is collected by exchanges and brokers at the point of trade, so individual investors would not have to file or pay it directly [S2].
The bill taxes derivatives, including futures, swaps, and options, by treating each payment as a separate taxable transaction, targeting the instruments most used by large institutional traders [S2].

The bill applies to US persons, US exchanges, and controlled foreign corporations, and directs the Treasury Secretary to write rules preventing trades from being routed through foreign entities to dodge the tax [S2].

analysis.who_pays: High-volume financial traders bear the direct cost: exchanges and brokers collect the tax, but the cost falls on the funds and firms doing the trading, and some of it would likely be passed on to investors in wider trading spreads or slightly higher fund costs. A 0.1% tax on every trade also raises the cost of ordinary investing marginally, though it is small compared to typical commissions and spreads. Critics of such taxes warn they can modestly reduce market liquidity.

drawbacks.text: The tax applies to every covered purchase, including retirement accounts and small investors' trades, so ordinary savers would bear a small share of the cost through their funds and brokers [S2].

A transaction tax can reduce trading volume and liquidity, which can slightly widen the spread between buying and selling prices, a cost borne by anyone trading, and some trading may shift to venues outside the tax's reach despite the anti-avoidance rules [S2].
The bill would raise trading costs during a five-year phase-in before reaching its full rate, meaning revenue would be modest in early years relative to its ultimate design [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The direct cost to a typical individual investor is small, at most $1 per $1,000 traded once fully phased in, while the tax concentrates its burden on the highest-volume traders. The main risks are that some trading migrates abroad or that fund expenses rise slightly. On balance the design is aimed at large financial actors, though no revenue is earmarked for any specific public use, so its benefit to ordinary people is only as good as the federal spending the revenue supports.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the House Ways and Means Committee in June 2025, and the committee has taken no further action on it.

narrative.text: Rep. Val Hoyle of Oregon introduced the Wall Street Tax Act of 2025 in the House on June 17, 2025, joined by eight Democratic cosponsors including Reps. Jayapal, McGovern, Tlaib, and Schakowsky [S1].
The bill was referred the same day to the House Committee on Ways and Means, the committee with jurisdiction over tax legislation, and no hearings, markups, or floor action have followed [S4].
The 119th Congress remains in session through January 2027, so the bill is still alive on paper but has shown no movement beyond its referral [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Financial trading firms and exchanges are better off so far, since the tax has not advanced and trading remains untaxed. Its sponsors have gained a stated position but no enacted policy.

sides.party_line_note: No vote has occurred and no floor opposition is recorded; all 10 sponsors and cosponsors are Democrats, and the bill has simply sat in committee with no recorded opposition action [S3].

industries.note: Firms that execute enormous numbers of small trades would pay the tax on every transaction, where even a 0.1% rate wipes out much of the margin on high-frequency strategies. Stopping the tax preserves their business model, which exists by capturing fractions of a cent on trades ordinary investors' orders flow through.

industries.industry: Hedge funds and institutional asset managers
industries.note: The bill taxes derivatives payments as separate transactions, hitting the futures, swaps, and options these funds use heavily. Its defeat leaves their hedging costs unchanged.

Exchanges and brokers would become the tax collectors under the bill, adding an administrative burden, but the more direct effect of the bill dying is that trading volumes stay untaxed and undepressed. The bill's failure removes both the compliance duty and the risk that the tax reduces trading activity on their venues.

Brokers would collect and remit the tax on trades they execute. Defeat of the bill spares them collection costs, while passage would have added a modest administrative duty rather than a direct revenue loss.

analysis.trajectory: The bill has been referred to the House Ways and Means Committee with no action since June 2025. Most tax bills without a hearing or markup by the committee's leadership do not advance, particularly bills from the minority party with no Republican cosponsors. Barring a shift in committee control or leadership priorities, it is likely to die at the end of the 119th Congress without a vote.
